The winner often sees an advantage other people treat as background. It might be a network, a position, or a cost pattern. The practical lesson is simple: before you copy what looks strong, ask where the real leverage is actually sitting. The answer is often less visible than the headline strength. It also keeps rewarding the right move after the first glance. That is why leverage matters.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The chapter argues that power in strategy is often hidden rather than obvious. David and Goliath becomes a strategy story because David refuses the kind of fight Goliath wants. Distance and mobility change the contest. Wal-Mart shows the same logic in business. Its advantage is not just one good store but the reinforcing network underneath the stores. Marshall and Roche extend the idea again by showing how one side can compete through asymmetric cost rather than direct matching. The chapter's point is that force does not come only from size or effort. It often comes from discovering the leverage point that changes how the contest works. Hidden structure matters because it keeps later moves from being equal. The same move is worth more once the contest is bent. That difference explains why leverage can outlast raw effort over time longer.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: Most people look for power in the loudest place: size, budget, muscle, market share. Rumelt looks for it where the situation bends. chapterBreakdown.direct:
The chapter defines strategic power as hidden leverage inside a situation rather than as brute strength by itself. David and Goliath becomes the opening example because David wins only after refusing the kind of fight that favors Goliath. Distance and mobility change the terms. The lesson is that effective power often appears when the contest is reframed.

Rumelt uses that case to correct a common mistake. Leaders often look for advantage by asking how to get more of what is already visible: more budget, more people, more speed, more scale. A strategist asks a harder question. What asymmetry or structural advantage would make one move count more than another?

Wal-Mart illustrates this through system design. Its edge did not come mainly from one excellent outlet. The network underneath the stores carried the advantage. Distribution and coordination reinforced local performance in a way rivals could not copy by lifting surface practices alone. That distinction explains why imitation is frequently weaker than it first appears.

Marshall and Roche show the same principle in competitive form. Their strategy against the Soviet Union did not rely on direct matching. It relied on using American technological strengths to impose higher costs on Soviet adaptation. That is hidden power expressed through asymmetric burden. One side gains not by mirroring the race, but by shaping it so the other side pays more for each step.

This is why strategy and force are not identical. A large rival can still be vulnerable if the contest can be shifted toward a different kind of advantage. A smaller rival can still fail if it accepts a head-on contest that rewards the opponent's strengths.

The chapter also keeps one threshold visible. Durable leverage is different from a clever trick. Real power can be reinforced through structure, position, or cost logic. A one-off surprise may win a moment and still fail as strategy. That distinction matters because the next chapter can now define bad strategy more sharply: it is not just vague. It is often blind to the leverage already available.
chapterBreakdown.competitive:
The chapter takes power out of the obvious places. Most people look first at scale, budget, muscle, or market share. Rumelt looks for where the situation bends. David and Goliath matters because David does not try to be stronger on Goliath's terms. He changes the fight until Goliath's strength matters less and his own advantages matter more.

That is the chapter's operating rule. Power in strategy is often hidden inside the structure of the contest. If you keep asking how to push harder in the same race, you may miss the asymmetry that makes the race worth redesigning.

Wal-Mart makes the point in system form. The real edge was not one efficient store. It was the reinforcing network beneath the stores. Rivals could copy what customers saw and still miss the machinery that made the visible edge sustainable. That is why imitation is so often expensive and disappointing. Copying the surface leaves the engine with the original owner.

Marshall and Roche push the lesson into open rivalry. Instead of matching Soviet force weapon for weapon, they looked for ways to make Soviet responses more expensive. That is leverage at a harsher level. The winning move is not always to outrun the rival directly. Sometimes it is to shape the race so the rival pays a worse price for staying in it.

This is what separates force from strategic power. Force is quantity. Strategic power is leverage. A smaller player with the right leverage can matter more than a larger player with none. A larger player that never sees the bend in the contest can still waste its size.

The chapter also draws a useful boundary. Cleverness is not enough. A trick that works once is not the same as a durable source of power. Real leverage keeps changing the contest after contact. It can be reinforced by design, position, or repeated cost pressure. If it cannot, the surprise may still be real, but the strategy is still weak.

That boundary sets up the next chapter perfectly. Once you accept that power often hides in asymmetry and structure, one mark of bad strategy becomes obvious: leaders who never discover the leverage that is already there. They stay on the wrong terms, copy the wrong things, and burn effort where it buys the least.
